item.title: Lateral Raises DO"S &DONT'S
item.description:
Feeling the lateral raise in your traps instead of your delts?
Save this post & use this cue next time you perform the side (lateral) raise 👇🏻
A lot of people initiate the movement by shrugging the shoulders when:
1. The weights are too heavy • 2. They’ve been executing it poorly from the beginning
Next time you perform the lateral raise, instead of thinking of lifting the dumbbells “up”, think of lifting the dumbbells “out”, like you are dragging them against the walls.
You don’t need heavy weights for this movement!
Your traps will still be involved to some degree in this movement, but your delts should be doing most of the work!
Let me know if this tip helps! 👇🏻
👉🏼Apply for 1:1 coaching: link is in my bio • . • . • . • #upperbody #upperbodyworkout #shoulderworkou

item.description: 🔥 Rear Delt Fly – Perfect Form for Maximum Muscle Activation Rear delt fly is often done wrong, turning into a back or trap exercise. item.description: YOU SHOULD TO KNOW THIS Bent Over Row PROPER FORM Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Grasp a barbell with an overhand grip, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart. Keep your elbows close to your body and maintain a neutral spine. Save and share with your gym buddy

The Real Difference Between Restarting and Returning to Fitness | FitTruth Co.
item.description: Restarting means going back to zero — new plan, clean slate, erase the history. Returning means coming back with everything you learned still intact. A restart asks you to forget. A return asks you to use what you know. Forgetting feels lighter, which is why most people choose it. But the history is the only information specific enough to make the next attempt different from the last one. Returning is harder. It's also more likely to work. #FitnessConsistency #RestartCycle #HowToStayConsistent #SustainableFitnessJourney #WomensFitnessJourney #SelfTrust #StopRestartingFitness #FitnessForBusyWomen #ConsistencyOverMotivation #FitnessMindset #ProgressNotPerfection #HealthyHabitsForWomen

item.title: Maximize Your Dumbbell Row: How Pull Direction Impacts Muscle Activation
item.description: Small adjustments in your dumbbell row technique can make a big difference in muscle engagement! Pulling toward your hips activates the latissimus dorsi, helping you build a wider, stronger back. Pulling toward your chest targets the upper back, rhomboids, trapezius, and rear deltoids for improved posture and definition. Tailor your pull direction to your fitness goals and unlock the full potential of this versatile exercise! #DumbbellRowGuide #BackMuscleActivation #StrengthTrainingTips

item.description: Fix your form on the barbell row✅ Adjust your stance to shoulder width and position your hand grip just slightly outside shoulder width, ensuring your thumb is over the bar instead of under. Maintain a neutral head position throughout the movement. Aim to achieve a 90-degree angle and focus on driving the weight upward and inward towards your belly button, rather than simply lifting straight up and down. #workout #homeworkout #homefitness #fitnes #gymvideos #gymtips #health #fitnesshealth #fitnessvideos #workoutvideos #exercisetips #workouttips #homeexercise #gymlife #gymquotes #gymmotivation #fitnessmotivation #exerciseplan #fitnesstips

item.title: BENT OVER TWO ARM LONG BAR ROW
item.description: Bent over two arm long bar row demo. For this exercise, you will need a Long Bar, a hard floor, and an obstruction-free space around you. The bent over two arm long bar row effectively targets the middle back, traps, biceps and triceps. It’s essentially a more concentrated version of the renegade row, as it doesn’t rely as much on the stabilizing muscles and arguably targets the arms further. Primary Movers: Trapezius, latissimus dorsi, deltoids, biceps, triceps Secondary Muscles: Forearms

item.title: Barbell Row Variations!
item.description: **Barbell Row Variations 💪🔥** Strengthen your back with different styles of barbell rows. The **standard bent-over row** targets your lats and upper back, while the **underhand barbell row** hits the lower lats and also works the biceps. For explosive power, try the **Pendlay row**, which starts from the floor each rep. The **Yates row** is done with a slight torso angle, focusing on the traps and rear delts. You can also do **T-bar rows using a barbell setup** to build mid-back thickness. Rotate these variations to build a strong, wide, and powerful back! 🏋️‍♂️🔥
item.content:encoded: **Barbell Row Variations 💪🔥** Strengthen your back with different styles of barbell rows. The **standard bent-over row** targets your lats and upper back, while the **underhand barbell row** hits the lower lats and also works the biceps. For explosive power, try the **Pendlay row**, which starts from the floor each rep. The **Yates row** is done with a slight torso angle, focusing on the traps and rear delts. You can also do **T-bar rows using a barbell setup** to build mid-back thickness. Rotate these variations to build a strong, wide, and powerful back! 🏋️‍♂️🔥

item.title: 10K reactions · 528 comments | Most People Row with Their Arms… and Miss the Entire Point. If you're trying to build a strong, defined back—but you're feeling rows in your biceps or shoulders—you’re doing it wrong. This video breaks down how to properly execute the kneeling cable row to actually target your lats, rhomboids, and traps—the muscles that should be doing the work. Key Tips: Think “pull with your elbows,” not your hands. Keep your shoulders down and back—no shrugging! Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end of the movement. It’s not about how heavy you go—it’s about how well you connect with the muscle. Master this movement, and your back will start popping from every angle. Here’s how to fix it: 1. Pull with your elbows, not your hands. 2. Keep shoulders down and back. 3. Squeeze your shoulder blades together like you're pinching a pencil. This kneeling cable row variation puts you in the perfect position to connect with your lats and stop letting your biceps steal the work. Form over ego = real muscle. Watch. Learn. Apply. Your back will thank you later. #FitNationApproved #BackDayTips #CableRowForm #BodybuildingTips #FormCheck #MuscleConnection Drop a comment if you’ve been guilty of rowing with your biceps—no shame, we’ve all been there! | Dee Jackson | Facebook

item.title: Back Strength Workout
item.description:
This dumbbell workout will strengthen your back and improve your posture. I am using two 6 kilogram weights. Which is a medium arm weight for me. You can always modify by doing single arms and alternating. Or if you are up for the challenge do both arms at once!
3 sets of 12 of each exercise • Rear Flys • Reverse Grip Bent Over Narrow Row • Narrow Rows • Wide Rows
Last Move only one time for 1 minute!
Single Dumbbell narrow row speed burnout!
Form tip* when you are hinged forward it is important to engage your core and keep a flat back and an open chest.
@lindsayrosebush
Workout with me https://youtube.com/@PilatesOnDemand

item.title: How To Do Pendlay Rows Correctly
item.description: Unlike the way most people perform the bent over row - from a hanging position with the weight never touching the ground during a set, each rep of the Pendlay row starts with the weight on the ground. This enforces strict form, encourages the correct posture, and minimizes momentum. The strict form not only reinforces better form, but improves its carry over to weightlifting-specific movements and pulls.

Dumbbell Row Form Tips Maintain Forearm Angle:
item.description: Dumbbell Row Form Tips Maintain Forearm Angle: Keep your forearms perpendicular to the floor, aiming for a 90-degree or wider angle between your upper arm and forearm, at the top of the movement. This helps reduce biceps involvement, keeping the focus on your back muscles.Avoid Upper Body Twist: As you lift the dumbbell, keep your torso stable. Twisting creates momentum and can shift tension to your lower back instead of your lats. Depress Your Shoulders: Keep your shoulders down to prevent engaging the traps. This ensures the lats bear most of the load. Use a Curved Path: Pull the dumbbell in a smooth, curved path from the floor toward your waist. This optimizes the range of motion and targets the lats effective

item.title: Supinated Bent Over Row: Basic Execution Guide
item.description: The supinated bent over row, also known as the underhand bent over row, is a compound exercise that primarily targets the muscles of the back while also engaging the biceps and core. Unlike its pronated counterpart, the supinated grip (palms facing up) allows for a greater range of motion and increased activation of the lower lats and biceps. To perform this exercise, start by standing with your feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent. Hinge at the hips, lowering your torso until it's nearly parallel to the floor. Grasp the barbell with an underhand grip, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width. From this position, pull the bar towards your lower chest or upper abdomen, squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the movement. Lower the bar back down with control to com

item.title: One arm dumbbell row 1. Using a neutral grip, pick up the dumbbell with one hand. Pull your shoulder blade back while ke
item.description: One arm dumbbell row 1. Using a neutral grip, pick up the dumbbell with one hand. Pull your shoulder blade back while keeping your arm straight. This is the starting position for the exercise. 2. Slowly pull the dumbbell up as far as possible. 3. Pause and squeeze your shoulder blades together, and then slowly lower the dumbbell back to starting position. 4. Repeat 10 to 12 times and then repeat on your other side.

item.title:
DUMBBELL ROW: STOP TWISTING YOUR BODY! ❌
A common mistake during the one-arm dumbbell row is rotating the torso and shrugging the shoulder to move more weight. It may help you lift a heavier dumbbell, but it reduces the work your lats are actually doing.
❌ Wrong: Twisting the torso + shrugging the shoulder = more momentum, more upper-trap involvement, less lat tension.
✅ Fix it: Keep your hips and shoulders square and stable, brace your core, then drive your elbow back toward your hip. Con...

item.title: How to do a bent over row?
🏋️‍♂️Know the difference between dumbbell bent over rows!💯⬇️
item.description: 🏋️‍♂️Know the difference between dumbbell bent over rows!💯⬇️ ✅ In the first option, I precisely hit the widest. What am I doing? ➡️ I turn on the core muscles (I tense up so that there is no arching in the lower back) ➡️ I stretch my lat forward (I move my shoulder and arm forward) ➡️ I start the movement first at the shoulder → scapula → bring my arm parallel to the floor ❌ In this version, you will not feel your back, and your arms will fall off. Since the movement occurs only due to the triceps, posterior deltoids, upper trapezius... but not due to the latissimus muscle! 💫Follow for daily motivation, gym, and fitness tips 🏋️💪 ... .. . #fit #fitfam #fitness #fitnessaddict #fitnessgirl #fitnessjourney #Glutes🍑 #usa #legdayworkout #legdayworkouts #legday🍑 #legdays #legworkout

item.title: Core Bracing Routine For Lifters -- 6 Moves To Protect Your Spine Under Load
item.description: A strong brace keeps the spine rigid under a heavy bar -- without it, force leaks through a rounding back instead of into the lift. In order: hollow hold, dead bug, pallof press, farmer carry, bird dog, side plank. Practice bracing hard for each rep the same way you would before a heavy set. About 8 minutes, done before you lift. Stretchr builds your daily mobility routine around exactly this kind of work.

item.title: THE BEST WAY TO DO BENT OVER ROWS
item.description:
CHEST SUPPORTED ROWS DETAILS:
1️⃣ The benefit of adding the bench is to keep your knees and hips and torso mostly still to isolate your back as well as decreasing the need to stabilize your lower back.
2️⃣ Scoop your elbow. Avoid pulling your elbows straight up ↕️ but instead with “scooping” motion bring your elbow back and up so you’re able to target the lats better. Stop when your elbow is just past your torso
3️⃣ Keep a neutral spine by tucking your pelvis, and letting feet relax behind you helping with hold your stance
